text: Visible username, user ID, login email, password, passcode, PIN, OTP, MFA token, authentication code, recovery code, or security-answer requests support Credential Theft.
A password field combined with account verification, session expiry, unusual activity, account locking, or security-check language is stronger evidence than a password field alone.
Requests to approve a push, enter a code from an authenticator app, provide an SMS code, or supply a backup code support theft of second-factor authentication secrets.
A fake single-sign-on, webmail, cloud-storage, workplace, or social-media login page can be used to harvest credentials when login secrets are visibly requested.

A document-sharing or attachment lure that asks the user to sign in before viewing a file supports Credential Theft, not Malware Distribution, unless a suspicious download or execution action is also visible.
A QR-code prompt that directs the user to sign in or verify an account supports Credential Theft when the surrounding screenshot explicitly references authentication.
Credential targets include email, cloud storage, social media, enterprise identity, banking, payment, e-commerce, and government-service accounts.
A logo, account warning, identity-verification message, or Confirm My Identity button without a visible request for authentication secrets is insufficient on its own to assign Credential Theft.
An email-address field used only for contact, delivery, receipt, newsletter, or account discovery is not automatically a login credential. Interpret the field using nearby labels and actions.
Strong Credential Theft evidence names the exact visible secret or authentication field instead of relying only on suspicious tone or brand imitation.
When credential fields appear with phone, address, date of birth, or government-ID fields, assign Credential Theft and Personal Information Harvesting if both sets are visibly supported.
If the current screenshot is only a pre-login warning or redirect page and the credential form is not visible, do not infer Credential Theft from a possible next page.
Visible requests for card number, CVV or CVC, expiry date, cardholder name, bank account, routing number, IBAN, transfer details, or wallet seed directly support Financial Fraud.

A payment or billing update request combined with failed delivery, unpaid invoice, subscription expiry, refund, tax, penalty, or suspicious-purchase language supports Financial Fraud when payment details or money transfer are visibly requested.
Requests to send money through wire transfer, gift cards, cryptocurrency, instant payment, or a new beneficiary support Financial Fraud.
A fake invoice or vendor-payment page can seek direct payment or altered bank details. Visible remittance instructions, amounts, account numbers, or payment controls support Financial Fraud.
A parcel redelivery or customs-fee page supports Financial Fraud when it visibly requests a fee or payment-card details.

A tax-refund or tax-debt page supports Financial Fraud when it visibly requests bank, card, transfer, or payment information; personal identity fields may additionally support Personal Information Harvesting.
Financial targets include payment cards, bank accounts, online wallets, merchant accounts, tax payments, invoices, refunds, investments, and cryptocurrency.
A PayPal, bank, card, invoice, shopping, or cryptocurrency logo does not by itself prove Financial Fraud. Require visible financial-data collection or a money-moving request.
A price, order summary, balance, transaction notice, or suspicious-purchase warning without a visible payment request is insufficient by itself for Financial Fraud.
Strong Financial Fraud evidence identifies the exact visible payment field, amount, transfer instruction, card request, account request, or payment button.
Payment-card or bank fields together with name, address, phone, date of birth, tax ID, or identity-document fields can support Financial Fraud and Personal Information Harvesting.
A sign-in form for a bank or payment service is Credential Theft when it requests authentication secrets; do not assign Financial Fraud unless financial details or a money-moving action are visible.
Visible prompts to download, open, install, execute, run, enable, update, repair, scan, or activate a file or application support Malware Distribution when the context is suspicious.
source: CISA phishing signs; Microsoft phishing protection

text: Requests to enable macros, allow content, disable antivirus, change security settings, or bypass warnings are strong malware-delivery indicators.
Fake browser, Flash, codec, antivirus, security, operating-system, or application update prompts can support Malware Distribution when installation is requested.
ClickFix-style instructions that ask the user to open Run, Terminal, PowerShell, Command Prompt, copy a command, paste a command, or execute a command strongly support Malware Distribution.
Unexpected PDF, Word, Excel, archive, script, calendar, email, shortcut, APK, installer, or executable attachments support Malware Distribution when the screenshot asks the user to open or run them.
source: CISA phishing signs; Microsoft phishing trends

text: A CAPTCHA, error, document preview, or verification page that instructs the user to run commands or install software can be a malware-delivery step.
Malware-delivery lures include invoices, tax forms, shipping documents, resumes, cloud documents, software updates, security alerts, meeting invitations, and media files.
A generic Download, View, Open, Continue, or Update button does not by itself prove Malware Distribution when no file type, installation, execution, attachment, or command instruction is visible.
Downloading an ordinary PDF, image, receipt, statement, or known application from a legitimate context is not automatically malware distribution.
Strong Malware Distribution evidence names the visible file, file type, installation instruction, execution action, macro request, security bypass, or command.
A malicious attachment or fake update that also asks for login credentials can support Malware Distribution and Credential Theft when both behaviours are visible.
If the screenshot only advertises a product or states that an update is available, without a suspicious download, install, run, enable, or command action, abstain from Malware Distribution.

Visible requests for full name, home address, telephone number, date of birth, place of birth, nationality, or demographic details support Personal Information Harvesting when the context is suspicious.
source: CISA phishing signs; Microsoft phishing protection

text: Visible requests for passport, national ID, social-security or national-insurance number, tax identifier, driver licence, voter ID, employee ID, or identity-document upload support Personal Information Harvesting.

Visible requests for employment, salary, education, family, health, insurance, biometric, or medical information support Personal Information Harvesting when unrelated to an expected legitimate process or already within a known phishing scope.
Identity-verification or KYC pages that request several identifiers, document images, selfies, addresses, dates of birth, or contact details can support Personal Information Harvesting.
Prize, survey, benefits, tax, job, delivery, refund, insurance, and account-recovery lures can harvest personal information when the screenshot visibly requests identity or contact data.
A form requesting unrelated or excessive identity details, such as passport and tax ID for a simple parcel fee, is stronger harvesting evidence than an expected minimal contact field.
Personal-information targets include identity, contact, demographic, employment, government, tax, insurance, healthcare, education, and family data.
A single name, contact-email, telephone, billing-address, delivery-address, or profile field can be legitimate. Do not assign Personal Information Harvesting solely from ordinary form presence.
A Confirm My Identity button or identity-warning message without visible personal-data fields or document requests is insufficient by itself for Personal Information Harvesting.
Strong Personal Information Harvesting evidence identifies the exact visible personal field, identity number, requested document, upload control, or excessive combination of fields.

Login secrets plus personal identity fields support Credential Theft and Personal Information Harvesting; payment details plus identity data support Financial Fraud and Personal Information Harvesting.
If personal information is implied but not visibly requested on the current screenshot, do not infer harvesting from a possible later form.
